evidence_quotes.quote: There was no significant difference in financial cost of water, school attendance, child health or water storage practices.
VEA produced large increases in access to and satisfaction with water and sanitation services, in self-reported hygiene and sanitation behaviour, and in measures of water governance.

Indices are calculated by rescaling each variable in each index (eg, handwashing) so that higher values imply better outcomes, then standardising relative to the control group, following Kling et al37. Effects are in standard deviation units.
We found no evidence of any intervention effects on any of the primary outcomes in subgroup analyses of South Kivu province.

This programme produced large increases in the percentage of households who use improved water sources and who use improved sanitation facilities, almost doubling access to improved water sources (from 43% to 83%)

headline_result_summary: In a cluster-randomised controlled trial across 121 rural clusters (328 surveyed villages; 1,312 households) in four conflict-affected provinces of the Democratic Republic of Congo, the national community-driven Healthy Villages & Schools (VEA) programme—which bundles participatory community mobilisation, formal Health Zone agreements and "Healthy Village" certification, elected village WASH committees, and ~US$4,000/village in water and sanitation infrastructure grants—substantially increased household use of an improved primary water source by 33 percentage points (95% CI 22 to 45; 83% vs 43% in controls) and an improved sanitation facility by 26 percentage points (95% CI 14 to 37; 46% vs 18%), while also increasing household water satisfaction (+0.64 SD, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.85) and village-level water governance (+1.33 SD, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.54) at a median 5 months post-intervention. However, pooled intention-to-treat effects were statistically null for daily water collection time (-3.0 min, 95% CI -19.7 to 13.6), daily water quantity collected (+2.3 L, 95% CI -4.2 to 8.7), the financial cost of water index (+0.13 SD, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.36), and the village-level water quality and access index (+0.13 SD, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.44), with marked heterogeneity across provinces (null on all four primary outcomes in South Kivu; increased collection time of +43 min in Kasai vs -61 min in Kasai Central; reduced water quantity of -13 L in Kasai Central).
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: 1. BUNDLED INTERVENTION (CANNOT ISOLATE GOVERNANCE ALONE): VEA combines institutional/governance reforms (formal community-Health Zone agreement, election and training of a village WASH committee, Community Action Plan for Maintenance, and official Chief Medical Officer "Healthy Village" certification) with ~US$2,000 for water infrastructure, ~US$2,000 for sanitation infrastructure, and ~US$3,000 for personnel/behaviour-change mobilisation per village. As the authors note (p. 9), the trial estimates the bundled at-scale package and cannot disaggregate governance/participation effects from direct infrastructure subsidies. Additionally, "water governance" (+1.33 SD, Table 3) is an OUTCOME of VEA rather than an independent treatment arm. 2. INDEX POLARITY RESCALING TRAP (TABLE 3 vs TABLE 2): All secondary summary indices in Table 3—including "Financial cost of water"—were rescaled per Kling et al. (2007) so that HIGHER values always imply BETTER outcomes (p. 5 and Table 3 note p. 7). A careless coder could misread +0.13 SD on "Financial cost of water" as higher water cost/worse affordability (and note it is statistically null anyway: 95% CI -0.10 to 0.36). Conversely, in Table 2, "Time to collect water (min)" is in raw minutes where HIGHER values mean WORSE time burden (-3.0 min pooled [null]; +43 min in Kasai = statistically significant WORSENING of collection time; -61 min in Kasai Central = significant IMPROVEMENT). 3. CO-PRIMARY & VILLAGE-LEVEL NULLS: Two of the four preregistered primary outcomes (collection time and water quantity collected, Table 2) and the village-level "Water quality and access" index (functional improved water points, N=328 villages, ITT = 0.13 SD, 95% CI -0.18 to 0.44, Table 3) are statistically null, despite the +33 pp gain in household-reported improved primary water source. 4. MINOR TEXT DISCREPANCIES: Abstract/p. 3 mention 332 candidate villages in 121 clusters, whereas p. 3 (Randomisation) and p. 6 (Results) clarify that after randomly dropping 7 villages to meet operational targets, the analysed sample is 328 villages (145 treatment, 183 control) and 1,312 households (580 treatment, 732 control) in 121 clusters. Also on p. 7, the parenthetical "(22% vs 9%)" after "9 pp less likely to report no facilities" swaps control and treatment order relative to the rest of the paragraph (control = 22%, treatment = 9%, matching 22 - 9 = 13 raw / ~9 pp adjusted).
study_design: Cluster-randomised controlled trial (cRCT) evaluated via intention-to-treat (ITT) linear regression models controlling for randomisation strata (province and number of villages per cluster) with cluster-robust standard errors, measured at a median of 5 months (151 days) post-intervention.
unit_and_sample_size: Randomisation unit: 121 clusters of rural villages (50 treatment clusters containing 145 surveyed villages; 71 control clusters containing 183 surveyed villages; 328 surveyed villages total). Primary analytic unit: 1,312 households (580 intervention, 732 control; 4 households per village; N = 1,260 households for school attendance index). Village-level outcomes (water governance; water quality and access): N = 328 villages (145 intervention, 183 control). Child health index: N = 1,388 children aged 10-59 months (646 intervention, 742 control).
